fragments.text: You cannot stuff 10,000 documents into the prompt. You need a smarter approach: send only the relevant ones.

slide_text: Instead of sending all documents, find the relevant one first , then send only that one to the model.

fragments.text: But how do you decide which document is relevant? The simplest idea: keyword matching.

slide_text: Part 3: When Words Lie
Build a tiny keyword search engine and watch it fail: [code block]

fragments.text: The sentence with the word hotel scores highest. But sentences about accommodation costs and lodging expenses which mean exactly the same thing score zero .

slide_text: The key idea: What if you could turn the meaning of a sentence into a list of numbers ?

fragments.text: Two sentences that mean the same thing produce similar lists of numbers . These number lists are called embeddings . But how do you measure similar between two lists of numbers?

Scenario Time per query Embed once, store 10ms (just the query) Re-embed per query 2.8 hours Embed documents once . At query time, only embed the question.

What you just invented: a vector index the data structure at the heart of systems like Pinecone, Weaviate, and pgvector. You embed documents once during indexing. At query time you only embed the question one embedding, not thousands.

slide_text: Part 5: Inventing RAG
Connect your two pieces: retrieval (Part 4) + language model (Part 1). [code block]

fragments.text: It works! The model answers from the actual documents.

slide_text: Now try this: [code block]

fragments.text: This question has nothing to do with Acme Corp policies. What happens?

The model answers from general knowledge , ignoring the retrieved context. It doesn t say I don t know. Even worse: the retrieved documents are irrelevant (maybe about IT security or something), and the model just ignores them.
Two fixes needed: Tell the model to answer only from the context Don t call the model at all when retrieval fails

slide_text: Your turn: Fix in two ways: Improve the prompt: Answer only using the context. If the answer is not there, say so. Add a confidence gate : if the top retrieval score is below 0.35, skip the API call entirely. Hint Check before building the prompt or calling the API.

Real documents are long. If you embed a 10-page PDF as one vector, the embedding averages out over too many topics. If you split every sentence separately, each piece loses context. There s a Goldilocks size. Hint . Loop with . Each chunk is .

fragments.text: Your turn: Write : split text into overlapping windows of ~ words.

slide_text: Experiment. Try different chunk sizes: [code block]

fragments.text: What do you observe? Too small means you lose context ( $250 separated from hotel ). Too large means the embedding averages over too many topics. A chunk of 50 150 words with 10 20% overlap is a common sweet spot.

slide_text: What you just invented: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) retrieve relevant chunks, gate on confidence, generate a grounded answer. This is the dominant architecture for grounding LLMs in private or recent knowledge. The confidence gate prevents hallucination when retrieval fails. Chunking with overlap prevents relevant sentences from being split across boundaries.

Quick Check A user asks What is the speed of light? None of your company documents are about physics. What happens? The model answers correctly from training data The model hallucinates using the closest document The confidence gate blocks it all scores are below 0.35 The system crashes

fragments.text: C. The confidence gate catches this. No document is relevant, so the fallback message is returned without calling the model at all . No hallucination, and you save on API costs.

slide_text: Part 6: The Model That Cannot Act
RAG solves the knowledge problem. But what about questions that require doing something? [code block]

Question What happens Current time Guesses or refuses can t check a clock 7 13 Might be wrong unreliable at arithmetic Stock price Outdated or made up can t access the web

slide_text: The model is sandboxed . It cannot interact with the outside world. It can only process text and return text.

fragments.text: But you can run a calculator. You can check the clock. What if the model could ask you to do it?
The model reasons . You execute . This is the key insight.

What would you need? A loop. Call a tool, feed the result back, let the model decide: do I need another tool, or can I answer now? Repeat.

slide_text: What you just invented: tool use (also called function calling ) the mechanism that lets a language model request external actions. The model is a reasoning engine , not an execution engine. It describes what tool to call as text. Your code parses that text, runs the function, and passes the result back.

slide_text: What you just invented: the agentic loop the core architecture of every AI agent. Also known as the ReAct pattern (Reasoning + Acting). The model itself is stateless. But the system around it the message history, the tool dispatcher, the memory store gives it the ability to reason over multiple steps, remember context, and take actions.

Reflection

Reflection Answer in your own words there are no right or wrong answers. In Part 1, you discovered hallucination. Why can t you detect it just by reading the model s output? In Part 3, keyword matching failed on synonyms. How do embeddings fix this? Could you explain a dot product to a friend who has never coded? In Part 5, you added a confidence gate. Why is it important to not call the model when retrieval fails? In Part 7, you turned a single tool call into a loop. What makes the loop an agent ? Explain RAG to someone in one sentence.

Going Further Vector databases. Replace your in-memory index with ChromaDB or Qdrant both have free local modes. Native tool use. The OpenAI API supports structured tool calling (function calling) the model returns JSON instead of the text protocol you invented. Rewrite your agent using it. Anthropic offers a similar feature called native tool use. The ReAct paper. Read ReAct: Synergizing Reasoning and Acting in Language Models (Yao et al., 2022). It describes the exact loop you built in Exercise 7.1. Evaluation. Use from to measure your agent s accuracy across 15 question-answer pairs. Multi-agent systems. What if one agent specialised in retrieval and another in calculation, with a coordinator deciding which to call?
